title: Graphic devices and patterns
instruction: Add dividers, frames, markers and watermarks only where they help someone read.
intro: A graphic device is a mark that helps a reader find their way: a divider between sections, a watermark, a marker on the place a reform acts, a key, a locator, a frame around a process. Each one has a job, and the page leaves it out where that job is already done.

Rules 12.1 to 12.3 cover the devices that divide and sign a page: hairlines, watermarks and the monogram as a small signature. Rule 12.4 says when an open area stays plain and what may sign it. Rules 12.5 to 12.9 cover the devices that explain a system: the intervention marker, which shows where a reform acts, chart keys, locators, the layer diagram and the frame that names who owns each step.

rules.title: Divide sections with a Stone hairline.
rules.rule: Between the sections and modules of a page, draw a 1 px hairline in the surface’s hairline color: Stone on Newsprint, White and Charcoal, and White on Prussian. Run it the width of the column it divides, with 24 px above and below. Where an article turns from how a decision is made to what a reader can do, the hinge divider takes the hairline’s place (Rule 04.4). Draw every divider solid.

why.text: A hairline separates two sections without weight, so the words carry the structure and the page stays calm. In our atlas a dashed line marks a connection graded plausible, so a dashed divider would read as a claim about the evidence. A hairline carries no meaning, so it needs no contrast ratio (Rule 05.5).
why.basis: Design judgment, carried from our fifth edition’s Stone hairlines

correct.caption: An article on a town budget at true size: a Stone hairline between its first two sections, the hinge divider before What you can do, and below, the hairline on each of the four surfaces.

failure.caption: The same article divided by dashed lines. The breaks now read as the atlas’s mark for a plausible connection, and the turn to the reader’s step loses its divider.

specs.label: Line
specs.value: 1 px, solid

specs.label: Color
specs.value: Stone on Newsprint, White and Charcoal; White on Prussian

specs.label: Length
specs.value: The width of the column it divides

specs.label: Space
specs.value: 24 px above and below

specs.label: The turn to a reader’s step
specs.value: The hinge divider (Rule 04.4)

specs.label: Never
specs.value: Dashed, dotted, doubled, red or shadowed

rules.builders: Draw the hairline as a 1 px top border on the section that follows, in the surface’s hairline token, so it follows the column’s width with no image.

rules.title: Set a watermark in an open margin, at its token opacity.
rules.rule: A watermark is ampersand B, drawn large from its display master and faint: Charcoal at 8 percent on Newsprint and White, and Newsprint at 10 percent on Charcoal and Prussian. It sits in an open margin of a report page or a dark section opener, and it may run off the page’s edge. It never sits behind words, a figure or a control. It counts as the view’s one ampersand moment (Rule 04.2), so a page with a hinge headline takes no watermark.

why.text: At 8 and 10 percent the mark measures 1.17 and 1.24 to 1 against its page, too faint to carry meaning, so it signs the page and asks nothing of the reader. Kept to an open margin, it never lowers the contrast of anything a reader needs. These two opacities are the only ones a page may use (Rule 05.6).
why.basis: Design judgment, carried from our fifth edition’s quiet signatures; the opacities are tokens

correct.caption: A report page on Newsprint and a section opener on Charcoal at true size, each with B in its open right margin, running off the right edge, which cuts through B’s loop and crossing stroke.

failure.caption: The report page with the watermark moved behind its heading and paragraph. Its edges cross the letters, and the words lose the clean ground they need.

specs.label: Mark
specs.value: Ampersand B, from its display master

specs.label: On Newsprint and White
specs.value: Charcoal at 0.08, 1.17 to 1

specs.label: On Charcoal and Prussian
specs.value: Newsprint at 0.10, 1.24 to 1

specs.label: Size
specs.value: At least half the page’s height; it may run off any edge

specs.label: Crop
specs.value: Where an edge cuts B, it cuts through strokes the eye can follow, with no piece of B left alone at the edge and no curve grazing it (Rule 04.8)

specs.label: Place
specs.value: An open margin of a report page or a section opener

specs.label: Never
specs.value: Behind words, a figure or a control; in red; beside a hinge headline or a crop of B

rules.builders: Set the opacity on the mark from its token, and place the mark in its own layer, outside the text column and hidden from assistive technology. Move it until every part of B inside the page joins the rest of the letter.

rules.title: Sign a small header or a video’s corner with L8 at full strength.
rules.rule: Where a page or a frame has room only for a small mark, such as a report’s running head or the corner of a video, sign it with L8, the monogram, opaque, from its 48 px minimum, in its colors for the surface (Rule 03.5). In a video, set it 24 px in from the frame’s edges.

why.text: A watermark shrunk to a corner falls under what an eye, or a compressed video, can hold, and it stops signing anything. At full strength and at its minimum, L8 keeps every letter and the ampersand’s two counters (Rule 03.4).
why.basis: Design judgment, from our fifth edition’s quiet signatures

correct.caption: A report’s running head on White with L8 at 48 px wide, and a still from an explainer video on Charcoal with L8 in its top right corner.

failure.caption: The video still with L8 at a watermark’s 10 percent. In the corner of a moving picture the mark all but vanishes.

specs.label: Mark
specs.value: L8, the monogram

specs.label: Size
specs.value: From 48 px wide (Rule 03.4)

specs.label: Color
specs.value: Rule 03.5: Charcoal with its red ampersand on Newsprint and White, Newsprint with it on Charcoal, all White on Prussian

specs.label: In a video
specs.value: 24 px in from the frame’s top and side edges

specs.label: Never
specs.value: At a watermark’s opacity, or as an avatar or a favicon

rules.builders: Export the video’s signature as a PNG at twice its size from the L8 master, with its colors written in, and keep it in the same corner for the whole video.

rules.title: Leave an open area plain, or sign it with the large crop of B or a watermark.
rules.rule: We use no repeating pattern. A cover or a section opener may carry the large crop of B (Rule 04.8), and a report page or a section opener may carry a watermark in its open margin (Rule 12.2). A social card, and any view whose ampersand moment is a hinge headline, keeps its open area plain.

why.text: Every shape we own already has a rule that a repeat would break: a view carries one ampersand moment (Rule 04.2), the lockmark always appears whole (Rule 08.3), and a row of nodes would read as the numbered steps that follow a bill (Rule 11.1). A pattern that avoids them has to use common shapes, so a cover that carries one looks like a stock report template. The crop of B and the watermark sign an open area with the ampersand from our wordmark.
why.basis: Design judgment, approved by our founder and editor in November 2026

correct.caption: The Report 3 cover at true size, signed with the large crop of B off its bottom-right corner, clear of the words.

failure.caption: Nothing on this cover says Oath & Action, and the arcs take the corner the crop of B would sign.

specs.label: Plain
specs.value: The first choice for an open area

specs.label: Crop of B
specs.value: A cover or a section opener, bottom right, at Rule 04.8’s measures

specs.label: Watermark
specs.value: A report page or a section opener, in the open margin, at Rule 12.2’s measures

specs.label: Kept plain
specs.value: A social card, and any view whose ampersand moment is a hinge headline (Rule 04.2)

specs.label: Never
specs.value: A repeating pattern of arcs, lines, dots, nodes or ampersands

rules.builders: Leave an open area plain by default. Sign it with the crop of B only on a cover or a section opener that holds no hinge headline, and check Rule 04.8’s measures on the cover at its true size.

rules.title: Mark where a reform acts with the atlas’s red target, and with nothing else in red.
rule: Where a figure shows a reform at work, the marks it acts on turn Pillar Red at a heavier weight: each connection it changes, with its arrowhead, and the outline of each variable it targets. A connection is the atlas’s arrow from one variable to another (Rule 10.10). On Newsprint a red connection carries a 1 px Charcoal edge. A note beside the figure names the reform and says that it acts where the marks turn red.

The marker is the view’s one working red. When an error or a step the reader can take now shares the view, the marker yields as Rule 11.16 sets out: its marks stay heavier, in ink, and the note still names the reform.

text: Red means one thing across the atlas: this is where a reform acts. It never marks a problem or a bad step, so a reader of any party can follow the mechanism without being told which outcome to dislike. The heavier weight and the note carry the meaning when red is gone, in gray print or beside an error. Pillar Red measures 2.96 to 1 on Newsprint, so a 1 px Charcoal edge, at 13.29 to 1, outlines the red line against the page.
why.basis: Design judgment, from the atlas’s visual system

correct.caption: Reform R‑01, all-party primaries with ranked general elections, on one step of Loop R10, the safe-seat loop: in red when it holds the view’s red, then in ink when an error does.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 12.5. Red marks the problem, and the note calls it one. The figure now takes a side on an outcome and spends the view’s red on it.

specs.label: Target weight
specs.value: Pillar Red: connections 4 px, variable outlines 3 px; arrowheads and sign tags at the 6 px sizes

specs.label: Edge on Newsprint
specs.value: 1 px Charcoal on each side of a red connection, as a 6 px case under the 4 px line

specs.label: Note
specs.value: “Reform R‑01, …, acts where the marks turn red.”

specs.label: Yielded
specs.value: The same weights in ink, with the note (Rule 11.16)

builders: Draw the marks with the atlas build’s own wire_marks and give the targets the kit’s ak-target class; the kit’s Newsprint surface sets the keyline. Set data-red="working" on the red marks so the check can count the view’s red.

rules.title: Label marks where they sit, and set a key above the chart only for what labels cannot carry.
rule: Name each line, bar or point beside it where the label fits. When a chart codes something a label cannot carry on every mark, such as the evidence grade of each segment, set a key above the plot. List its items in the order the marks run, draw each swatch in the chart’s own mark, give each its word and meaning, and name the unit in the measure line, the line under a chart’s title that says what is counted and in what unit.

text: A label beside its mark is read once. A key makes the reader look away, match a swatch and look back, so it should come before the plot, in the plot’s order, with swatches that match the marks exactly. Marks drawn as shades, a hatch and a dotted outline still tell the grades apart in gray print, where hues of the same lightness merge.
why.basis: Design judgment, from the chart system

correct.caption: A key above a phone chart, in the order the segments run, each swatch drawn as its mark. Its title says only what the counts show, that 28 of the 39 claims are documented or well supported.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 12.6. A boxed legend under the plot, in reverse order, with dots that match no mark and hues that merge in gray. The chart names no unit.

specs.label: Swatch
specs.value: 14 px, the label 7 px after it; items 16 px apart, wrapping in rows

specs.label: Order
specs.value: The order the marks run, left to right or top to bottom

specs.label: Grade marks
specs.value: In bars and areas, Documented solid ink, Well supported gray, Plausible light gray, Contested a hatch, Hypothesis a dotted outline; a connection in the atlas takes Rule 10.10’s line textures

specs.label: Place
specs.value: Under the title and measure line, above the plot

builders: Take the swatches and the grade table from the chart system’s build, key_item and GRADE_TABLE, so a key and its chart can never drift apart.

rules.title: Show where a view sits in the whole with a small locator in ink.
rule: A view that shows part of a larger whole carries a locator at its top right: the whole in small, with the current part filled in Charcoal and the rest in a light ground. In the atlas, the locator draws the atlas’s parts and links back to the overview. In a state story it is the 50-state tile grid.
Draw the locator in ink, with no red.

text: A reader who arrives from a search lands in the middle of the system. A locator answers “Where am I?” before the reader asks, and the same small map on every view teaches its shape. Kept to ink, it never competes with the red that marks a reform, an error or a step to take.
why.basis: Design judgment, from the atlas’s visual system

correct.caption: The atlas locator and the state locator at true size, each in ink, small enough that the headline beside it keeps at least 200 px on a phone.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 12.7. The current part filled red. “You are here” takes the view’s red, and the reform marker, the error or the ask loses it.

specs.label: Atlas locator
specs.value: 88 by 41 px, the parts as boxes, the current one filled

specs.label: State locator
specs.value: 8 px tiles with 1 px gaps, 12 columns, 107 by 71 px, the state filled; the headline beside it keeps at least 200 px on a 360 px phone

specs.label: Place
specs.value: Top right of the view’s header; hidden on phones in the atlas, where the breadcrumb carries it

specs.label: Ink
specs.value: Charcoal for the current part

builders: Draw the atlas locator from the atlas build’s locator() and the state locator from the tile grid file; mark the current part with a class, never with a color written into the drawing.

rules.title: Use an exploded view only to stack the atlas’s layers, and keep every name flat.
rule: An exploded view, a drawing of flat planes stacked at a slant, shows one thing in this guide: how the atlas’s three layers sit on one another. Draw each layer as a plane with one tile for each of its parts, join the planes with dotted ties, and set every name flat and upright beside its plane.

text: A slant shows depth, which suits layers and nothing else we draw. Names on a slant read slowly and turn to texture at small sizes, so the names stay flat where a reader’s eye already runs.

correct.caption: The atlas’s three layers, each with its parts, and every name flat beside its plane.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 12.8. The names follow the slant into the planes, so each one reads at an angle and the parts are lost.

specs.label: Planes
specs.value: Three, the core outlined at 2.5 px and the others at 1.5 px

specs.label: Ties
specs.value: 1 px dotted, two between each pair of planes

specs.label: Names
specs.value: Flat, upright, to the right of each plane, with a 1 px leader

builders: Read the layers and their parts from the atlas model, never from a list typed by hand, so the diagram follows the atlas when it changes.

rules.title: In a process explainer, name who owns the next step at every handoff.
rule: Give every step of a process a person or an office that acts, and at each handoff name who owns the next step and the deadline the law sets. Write each step with its actor first. Link the steps to the official procedure in a source line.

text: Our guide’s fourth edition put it in one line: “Give every handoff an owner.” A reader who knows who holds a request knows whom to call when it stalls. Passive steps hide that, and a process with no owner reads as one that runs by itself.
why.basis: Design judgment, from our guide’s fourth edition

correct.caption: A federal records request, with who acts at each step, who owns the next one and the deadline the law sets.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 12.9. Five passive boxes. The reader cannot tell who has the request or whom to call when it stalls.

specs.label: Each step
specs.value: Actor first, then the act

specs.label: Each handoff
specs.value: “Next step:” and the owner, then the deadline

specs.label: Source line
specs.value: The statute or official page for every deadline

builders: Name an office by its role, as in “the agency’s records office”, so the frame holds for every agency, and put the agency’s own name in a live page.
